walkthroughs.body_html:
Electric Circuits — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Electric Circuits brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Electric Circuits.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: If the separation between two point charges is halved, the force becomes:
options: Halved
Doubled
Quartered
Quadrupled

mcqs.q: The electric field between parallel plates 5.0 mm apart with a p.d. of 200 V is:
options: 1 kV m⁻¹
40 kV m⁻¹
100 V m⁻¹

mcqs.q: In which direction does an electric field point near a positive charge?
options: Radially outwards — the field is defined by the force on a positive test charge, which is repelled.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.
Adding a parallel resistor doubles the voltage available.
Radially inwards because positive attracts negative.

mcqs.q: What happens to the total resistance when you add another resistor in parallel?
options: Total resistance decreases — there are more paths for current to flow.
Adding any resistor always increases the total resistance.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.
Adding a parallel resistor doubles the voltage available.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
options: It halves — gravitational force is inversely proportional to distance.
It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
It quarters — gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
Adding a parallel resistor doubles the voltage available.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Uniform electric field”?
options: Field between parallel plates: E = V/d, with field lines straight and equally spaced.
Force per unit positive charge at a point: E = F/Q, measured in N C⁻¹ or V m⁻¹.
ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, characterising vacuum's ability to permit electric fields.
Surface on which electric potential is constant; no work is done moving along it.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Permittivity of free space”?
options: Field between parallel plates: E = V/d, with field lines straight and equally spaced.
Force per unit positive charge at a point: E = F/Q, measured in N C⁻¹ or V m⁻¹.
ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, characterising vacuum's ability to permit electric fields.
Work done per unit charge to bring a positive charge from infinity: V = Q/(4πε₀r).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Equipotential surface”?
options: Field between parallel plates: E = V/d, with field lines straight and equally spaced.
Force between point charges: F = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r²).
Work done per unit charge to bring a positive charge from infinity: V = Q/(4πε₀r).
Surface on which electric potential is constant; no work is done moving along it.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Coulomb's law”?
options: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, characterising vacuum's ability to permit electric fields.
Force between point charges: F = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r²).
Work done per unit charge to bring a positive charge from infinity: V = Q/(4πε₀r).
Field between parallel plates: E = V/d, with field lines straight and equally spaced.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Electric field strength”?
options: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, characterising vacuum's ability to permit electric fields.
Surface on which electric potential is constant; no work is done moving along it.
Force per unit positive charge at a point: E = F/Q, measured in N C⁻¹ or V m⁻¹.
Work done per unit charge to bring a positive charge from infinity: V = Q/(4πε₀r).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Electric potential”?
options: ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹, characterising vacuum's ability to permit electric fields.
Force between point charges: F = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r²).
Work done per unit charge to bring a positive charge from infinity: V = Q/(4πε₀r).
Force per unit positive charge at a point: E = F/Q, measured in N C⁻¹ or V m⁻¹.
